title: Leviticus 7:11–21
context: Leviticus 7:11–21 gives the law of the peace offering in its three kinds: thanksgiving, vow, and freewill offering. These were the offerings the worshiper shared in eating. Thanksgiving meat must be eaten the same day, and vow and freewill meat by the second day, with leftovers burned on the third. Eating in a state of uncleanness brings the penalty of being ‘cut off’. Both traditions see fellowship with God as a gift to be received with gratitude and reverence, and many readers connect it with the Lord’s Supper (1 Corinthians 11:27–29).

verses.text: “ ‘This is the law of the sacrifice of peace offerings, which one shall offer to the LORD:
verses.arminianNotes: The ‘law of the sacrifice of peace offerings’ introduces the fellowship meal, in which God, priest, and worshiper all share. Arminians see restored communion with God as the heart of worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree that the peace offering expresses fellowship already established by God’s covenant grace. Both traditions connect this shared meal with the communion believers enjoy through Christ.

verses.text: If he offers it for a thanksgiving, then he shall offer with the sacrifice of thanksgiving unleavened cakes mixed with oil, and unleavened wafers anointed with oil, and cakes mixed with oil.
verses.arminianNotes: Thanksgiving offerings include unleavened cakes and wafers with oil. Arminians see gratitude as a fitting, freely offered response to God’s goodness (compare Psalm 50:14).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree that thanksgiving is the believer’s fitting response to grace already received. Both traditions connect this with Hebrews 13:15, the ‘sacrifice of praise’ offered through Christ.

verses.text: He shall offer his offering with the sacrifice of his peace offerings for thanksgiving with cakes of leavened bread.
verses.arminianNotes: Leavened bread is included with the thanksgiving offering. Arminians note that it was eaten rather than burned on the altar, which is consistent with 2:11–12.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters make the same observation. Both traditions see the leavened bread as part of the shared meal and avoid forcing a symbolic meaning onto the leaven that the text does not state.

verses.text: Of it he shall offer one out of each offering for a heave offering to the LORD. It shall be the priest’s who sprinkles the blood of the peace offerings.
verses.arminianNotes: One of each kind of bread goes to the priest who sprinkles the blood, as a heave, or contribution, offering. Arminians see the worshiper’s gratitude shared with God’s servants.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same provision for the officiating priest. Both traditions read ‘heave offering’ as a portion lifted or set apart for God and given to the priest, and they agree on the verse.

verses.text: The flesh of the sacrifice of his peace offerings for thanksgiving shall be eaten on the day of his offering. He shall not leave any of it until the morning.
verses.arminianNotes: Thanksgiving meat must be eaten the same day, with nothing left until morning. Arminians see the joyful, immediate celebration of God’s goodness, likely shared widely with family and others.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree that the time limit keeps the meal holy and probably encouraged generous sharing. Both traditions read the verse as reverent celebration.

verses.text: “ ‘But if the sacrifice of his offering is a vow, or a free will offering, it shall be eaten on the day that he offers his sacrifice. On the next day what remains of it shall be eaten,
verses.arminianNotes: Vow and freewill offerings may be eaten on the day of offering or the next day. Arminians note that freewill offerings reflect the worshiper’s voluntary devotion, warmly welcomed by God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree that the freewill offering expresses a willing heart. Both traditions see the different time limits as part of God’s ordered worship and agree on the verse.

verses.text: but what remains of the meat of the sacrifice on the third day shall be burned with fire.
verses.arminianNotes: What remains on the third day must be burned. Arminians see the limit as protecting the sacred meal from decay and casual handling.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree that the rule guards the offering’s holiness. Both traditions note that practical concerns and holiness concerns may overlap, without claiming more than the text says.

verses.text: If any of the meat of the sacrifice of his peace offerings is eaten on the third day, it will not be accepted, and it shall not be credited to him who offers it. It will be an abomination, and the soul who eats any of it will bear his iniquity.
verses.arminianNotes: Meat eaten on the third day is not accepted or ‘credited’, is an ‘abomination’, and the eater bears iniquity. Arminians note that disobedience can turn a gift of worship into guilt, so worshipers are accountable for how they come.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the reckoning language (‘credited’) and stress that worship must follow God’s word to be acceptable. Both traditions agree that the verse concerns acceptance of the offering, and neither reads it as a direct statement about justification.

verses.text: “ ‘The meat that touches any unclean thing shall not be eaten. It shall be burned with fire. As for the meat, everyone who is clean may eat it;
verses.arminianNotes: Meat that touches anything unclean is burned, but anyone clean may eat. Arminians see God welcoming his people to the meal while requiring purity.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree on both points: a broad invitation to the clean and a guard against defilement. Both see an echo in the call to approach God’s table reverently.

verses.text: but the soul who eats of the meat of the sacrifice of peace offerings that belongs to the LORD, having his uncleanness on him, that soul shall be cut off from his people.
verses.arminianNotes: Eating the LORD’s peace offering while unclean brings being ‘cut off from his people’. Arminians take the warning seriously as real accountability for covenant members who treat holy things with contempt, and many relate it to 1 Corinthians 11:27–29.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also take the warning seriously and connect it to 1 Corinthians 11:27–29. Both traditions take the penalty seriously, though interpreters differ on whether ‘cut off’ meant exclusion from the community, premature death, or direct divine judgment.

verses.text: When anyone touches any unclean thing, the uncleanness of man, or an unclean animal, or any unclean abomination, and eats some of the meat of the sacrifice of peace offerings which belong to the LORD, that soul shall be cut off from his people.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: Touching uncleanness, whether human, animal, or any abomination, and then eating brings the same penalty. Arminians note that the law teaches personal responsibility to keep oneself fit for worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and stress that uncleanness here is ritual, not necessarily moral. Both see the verse fulfilled in Christ’s cleansing of his people (Hebrews 9:13–14).
